sectionTitle: Using concentrations of solutions in mol/dm 3 (chemistry only) (HT only)

specStatements.text: The concentration of a solution can be measured in mol/dm³ .
The amount in moles of solute or the mass in grams of solute in a given volume of solution can be calculated from its concentration in mol/dm³ .
If the volumes of two solutions that react completely are known and the concentration of one solution is known, the concentration of the other solution can be calculated.
Students should be able to explain how the concentration of a solution in mol/dm³ is related to the mass of the solute and the volume of the solution.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every concept, misconception and question in this section is tiered higher, matching the (HT only) marking carried by the whole of 4.3.4, so no item here is ever put in front of a Foundation tier student. The (chemistry only) marking is honoured by keeping this material out of any Combined Science route: concentration in mol/dm³, and the titration-style calculation built on it, appear only in this GCSE Chemistry section and are not treated as shared content.

scopeNotes.statement: If the volumes of two solutions that react completely are known and the concentration of one solution is known
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The statement licenses the calculation only when both volumes and one concentration are known, so every item of this kind (q08, q09, q10, q12) supplies both volumes, one concentration and the balanced symbol equation, and asks only for the unknown concentration. No item asks students to carry out or design a titration, to choose an indicator, to judge an end point experimentally, or to work with concordant titres, since none of that is contained in 4.3.4.

concepts.definition: A measure of how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution. The concentration of a solution can be measured in mol/dm³, which states the amount of solute, in moles, present in each 1 dm³ of solution.

The unit 'moles per decimetre cubed'. A concentration of 0.100 mol/dm³ means that every 1 dm³ of the solution contains 0.100 mol of solute. The unit describes the solution as a whole, so any portion taken from it has the same concentration.

The solute is the substance dissolved; the volume used in a concentration in mol/dm³ is the volume of the final solution, not the volume of water added to make it. A solid dissolved and made up to 1 dm³ of solution gives a solution whose volume is 1 dm³.

1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so a volume measured in cm³ is divided by 1000 to give the volume in dm³. For example 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³. Because the unit of concentration is mol/dm³, volumes must be in dm³ before they are used in any concentration calculation.

concepts.term: Amount of solute in a given volume
concepts.definition: The amount of solute, in moles, in a given volume of solution is found from the concentration: amount (mol) = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume of solution (dm³). This follows directly from the meaning of mol/dm³ as moles of solute per 1 dm³.

concepts.term: Mass of solute in a given volume
concepts.definition: Once the amount of solute in moles is known, its mass is found using the relative formula mass: mass (g) = amount (mol) × relative formula mass. Combining the two steps, mass of solute = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³) × relative formula mass.

The mass of solute dissolved in each 1 dm³ of solution. It is linked to the concentration in mol/dm³ by the relative formula mass: concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass. The same concentration in mol/dm³ therefore gives different g/dm³ values for different solutes.

concepts.term: Mole ratio from the balanced equation
concepts.definition: The balancing numbers in a balanced symbol equation give the ratio in which the substances react in moles. In H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O the ratio is 1 mol of sulfuric acid to 2 mol of sodium hydroxide, and this ratio converts the known amount of one solute into the amount of the other.

Two solutions react completely when the amounts of the two solutes are in exactly the ratio given by the balanced equation, so neither is left over. Knowing the two volumes that react completely, and the concentration of one solution, fixes the concentration of the other.

For a fixed mass of solute, making the solution up to a larger volume gives a smaller concentration in mol/dm³, because the same amount of solute is spread through more solution. Adding water changes the concentration but not the amount of solute present.

misconceptions.question: A solution of sodium hydroxide has a concentration of 0.250 mol/dm³. Is its concentration also 0.250 g/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)
misconceptions.correct: No. Each 1 dm³ contains 0.250 mol of sodium hydroxide, and 0.250 mol has a mass of 0.250 × 40 = 10.0 g, so the concentration is 10.0 g/dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: mol/dm³ and g/dm³ are just two ways of writing the same concentration, so the number stays the same when the unit changes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both units end in '/dm³', which makes them look like alternative labels for one quantity, in the way that 'cm' and 'centimetres' are. Students also meet g/dm³ and mol/dm³ in the same lesson and copy the same number into both columns of a table.
misconceptions.correction: Moles and grams are different quantities, so the two concentrations are different numbers. The relative formula mass converts between them: concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass.

misconceptions.question: A student calculates the amount of solute in 250 cm³ of a 0.200 mol/dm³ solution as 0.200 × 250 = 50 mol. What is wrong?
misconceptions.correct: The volume must be in dm³. 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³, so the amount is 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol.
misconceptions.misconception: The volume can be put into the calculation in whatever unit it was measured in, so 250 cm³ can be used as 250.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Volumes in the laboratory are always measured in cm³, so cm³ is the number the student has in front of them. The unit of concentration is written on the bottle rather than in the working, so its 'per dm³' part is easy to overlook.
misconceptions.correction: Read the unit of concentration first: mol/dm³ means moles in every 1 dm³, so the volume must be converted to dm³ by dividing by 1000 before it is used. An answer of 50 mol of solute in a quarter of a litre should also look impossible.

misconceptions.question: What is 250 cm³ in dm³?
misconceptions.correct: 0.250 dm³, because 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so cm³ are divided by 1000.
misconceptions.misconception: To change cm³ into dm³ you multiply by 1000, because dm³ is the bigger unit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the factor 1000 but not its direction, and reason that a 'bigger' unit should give a bigger number. The same slip converts mol/dm³ to g/dm³ by multiplying by 1000 instead of by the relative formula mass.
misconceptions.correction: A decimetre cubed is larger than a cubic centimetre, so any volume contains fewer dm³ than cm³ and the number must get smaller. Divide by 1000 going from cm³ to dm³, and multiply by 1000 going the other way.

misconceptions.question: 5.85 g of sodium chloride is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. Water is then added to make 1.00 dm³ of solution. Has the amount of sodium chloride in the flask changed?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is still 0.100 mol of sodium chloride; only the concentration has changed, from 0.400 mol/dm³ to 0.100 mol/dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding water to a solution reduces the amount of solute in it, because the solution becomes weaker.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language treats 'weaker' and 'less' as the same idea, and diluting a drink does make each mouthful contain less. The distinction between the total amount in the flask and the amount per dm³ is easily lost.
misconceptions.correction: No solute leaves the flask when water is added, so the amount in moles is unchanged. What changes is the volume of solution, and therefore the amount of solute per 1 dm³, which is the concentration.

misconceptions.question: Flask A holds 1.00 dm³ of copper sulfate solution and flask B holds 100 cm³ of copper sulfate solution. Which is the more concentrated?
misconceptions.correct: The volumes alone do not say. The concentration depends on the amount of solute in each dm³ of solution, so the amount of dissolved copper sulfate in each flask must also be known.
misconceptions.misconception: The flask with the larger volume of solution must have the higher concentration, because there is more of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More' is read as 'more concentrated'. Diagrams that show a large beaker of dark solution next to a small one reinforce the idea that size and strength go together.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration is a ratio, not a total. It compares the amount of solute with the volume of solution it is spread through, so a small flask can easily be more concentrated than a large one.

misconceptions.question: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Do the two solutions have the same concentration?
misconceptions.correct: No. Equal volumes react, but 2 mol of sodium hydroxide are needed for every 1 mol of sulfuric acid, so the acid concentration is half the alkali concentration.
misconceptions.misconception: If equal volumes of two solutions react completely together, the two solutions must have the same concentration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most worked examples in class use reactions in a 1:1 ratio, where equal volumes really do mean equal concentrations, and the balanced equation is never needed. The pattern is then generalised.
misconceptions.correction: Compare amounts in moles, not volumes. Work out the amount of the known solute, convert it using the mole ratio in the balanced equation, then divide by the volume of the other solution in dm³.

misconceptions.question: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by 12.5 cm³ of sulfuric acid. A student writes 0.100 × 25.0 = c × 12.5 and gets 0.200 mol/dm³. What has been missed?
misconceptions.correct: The mole ratio. The amount of sodium hydroxide is 0.00250 mol, so the amount of sulfuric acid is 0.00250 ÷ 2 = 0.00125 mol, giving 0.00125 ÷ 0.0125 = 0.100 mol/dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: You can always set concentration × volume for one solution equal to concentration × volume for the other, whatever the equation says.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The shortcut works for every 1:1 example and is often half-remembered from a formula sheet. Because it removes the need to look at the equation, students stop reading the balancing numbers at all.
misconceptions.correction: The equality of concentration × volume only holds when the two solutes react in a 1:1 ratio. Always find the amount in moles of the known solution, then use the balancing numbers to get the amount of the other.

misconceptions.question: A solution contains 0.0500 mol of sodium hydroxide (relative formula mass 40). What mass of sodium hydroxide is this?
misconceptions.correct: 2.00 g, because mass = amount × relative formula mass = 0.0500 × 40.
misconceptions.misconception: To get from moles to grams you divide the amount by the relative formula mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn 'moles = mass ÷ Mr' first and then reuse the division when going the other way, instead of rearranging it. The very small answer this produces is rarely checked for sense.
misconceptions.correction: Moles and mass are linked by one relationship: mass = amount × relative formula mass, and amount = mass ÷ relative formula mass. Going from moles to grams multiplies, and the answer should be larger, not smaller.

misconceptions.question: A student pours 25.0 cm³ from a bottle of 0.200 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide solution. What is the concentration of the 25.0 cm³ sample?
misconceptions.correct: 0.200 mol/dm³, exactly as in the bottle. Only the amount of solute is smaller: 0.200 × 0.0250 = 0.00500 mol.
misconceptions.misconception: Taking a smaller volume out of a bottle gives a solution of lower concentration, because there is less of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Amount and concentration are again being merged. It is true that the sample contains less solute, and students transfer that reduction to the concentration as well.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration is a property of the solution itself, not of how much of it you take. Every portion of a well-mixed solution has the same amount of solute per dm³, however small the portion is.

misconceptions.question: Two solutions are each made using 5.85 g of sodium chloride, one made up to 250 cm³ and the other to 1.00 dm³. Do they have the same concentration?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both contain 0.100 mol of sodium chloride, but the concentrations are 0.400 mol/dm³ and 0.100 mol/dm³, because the volumes of solution are different.
misconceptions.misconception: The concentration is decided by the mass of solute you weigh out, so the same mass always gives the same concentration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Weighing out the solid is the step the student performs and remembers; making up to the mark feels like a procedural detail rather than part of the quantity being defined.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration in mol/dm³ depends on two things: the amount of solute, found from its mass and relative formula mass, and the volume of the solution it is dissolved in. Change either one and the concentration changes.

misconceptions.question: 4.00 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 500 cm³. Which volume is used to find the concentration in mol/dm³?
misconceptions.correct: The 500 cm³ of solution, that is 0.500 dm³, giving 0.100 ÷ 0.500 = 0.200 mol/dm³.
misconceptions.misconception: The volume in the calculation is the volume of water you added to dissolve the solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In practical work the water is what is poured in and noticed, and for dilute solutions the two volumes are nearly the same, so the distinction seems not to matter.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration in mol/dm³ is amount of solute per 1 dm³ of solution. The solution is made up to a marked volume in a volumetric flask, and it is that final volume of solution that is used.

misconceptions.question: 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid exactly neutralises 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution. A student writes 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol. What has gone wrong?
misconceptions.correct: The known concentration belongs to the acid, so it must be used with the acid volume: 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol of hydrochloric acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Any of the volumes in the question can be used with the concentration you are given, because both solutions react together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two volumes and one concentration are on the page, and the numbers are not labelled with the substance they belong to once they are copied into the working. The wrong pairing still gives a plausible-looking answer.
misconceptions.correction: Label every value with its substance before calculating. The first step uses the concentration and the volume of the same solution; the other volume is only used at the final step, for the solution whose concentration is unknown.

misconceptions.question: How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
misconceptions.misconception: There are 100 cm³ in 1 dm³, because there are 10 cm in a decimetre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The conversion factor for lengths is applied once, or squared, instead of cubed. Students also recall '100' from the centi- prefix used for centimetres and metres.
misconceptions.correction: Cubing a length cubes the conversion factor: 1 dm³ = (10 cm)³ = 1000 cm³. It is worth checking against the familiar fact that 1 dm³ is 1 litre, which is 1000 cm³.

misconceptions.question: How is the amount of solute in a given volume of solution found from the concentration in mol/dm³?
misconceptions.misconception: Because concentration is moles divided by volume, you divide the concentration by the volume to get the moles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The division in the defining relationship is remembered, but the rearrangement is not carried out. Dividing by a volume smaller than 1 dm³ also makes the answer larger, which can look convincingly like 'more solute'.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging concentration = amount ÷ volume gives amount = concentration × volume. Check the units: mol/dm³ multiplied by dm³ leaves mol, which is what is wanted.

misconceptions.question: In H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, 0.00250 mol of sodium hydroxide reacts. What amount of sulfuric acid reacts?
misconceptions.correct: 0.00125 mol, because 2 mol of sodium hydroxide react with 1 mol of sulfuric acid, so the amount of acid is half the amount of alkali.
misconceptions.misconception: The 2 in front of NaOH means you multiply by 2 to get the amount of acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The balancing number is seen next to the substance being converted from, and multiplying feels like the natural use of it. Which way round the ratio goes is not checked against the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Read the ratio as a sentence: 1 mol of H₂SO₄ reacts with 2 mol of NaOH. So the amount of acid is the amount of alkali divided by 2, and the acid amount must come out smaller.

mcqs.stem: A bottle of sodium hydroxide solution is labelled 0.500 mol/dm³. What does this label tell you?

options.text: Each 1 dm³ of the solution contains 0.500 mol of dissolved sodium hydroxide.
options.rationale: A concentration in mol/dm³ states the amount of solute, in moles, present in every 1 dm³ of solution.

options.text: Each 1 dm³ of the solution contains 0.500 g of dissolved sodium hydroxide.
options.rationale: Students who treat mol/dm³ and g/dm³ as interchangeable labels keep the number and swap the unit.

options.text: Each 1 cm³ of the solution contains 0.500 mol of sodium hydroxide.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who do not attend to the volume unit in mol/dm³ and default to the cm³ used in the lab.

options.text: Each 1 dm³ of water added held 0.500 mol of sodium hydroxide.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think the volume in a concentration is the volume of solvent added rather than of solution.

mcqs.stem: A student measures out 25.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid solution. What volume, in dm³, must be used in a concentration calculation?

options.rationale: Multiplying by 1000 instead of dividing, on the reasoning that dm³ is the larger unit so the number should grow.
1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so 25.0 cm³ is divided by 1000 to give 0.0250 dm³.
Follows from believing 1 dm³ = 100 cm³ because there are 10 cm in a decimetre.
Comes from dividing by 10, using the linear centimetre-to-decimetre factor once and not cubing it.

mcqs.stem: A sodium chloride solution has a concentration of 0.200 mol/dm³. What amount of sodium chloride, in mol, is present in 250 cm³ of this solution?

options.rationale: The volume is used in cm³ without conversion: 0.200 × 250.
The concentration is divided by the volume, 0.200 ÷ 0.250, instead of multiplied by it.
250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³, and amount = concentration × volume = 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol.
Both errors together: dividing rather than multiplying and leaving the volume in cm³, 0.200 ÷ 250.

mcqs.stem: What mass of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in 500 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)

options.rationale: The volume is used as 500, giving 50 mol, which is then multiplied by 40.
The amount is divided by the relative formula mass instead of multiplied by it.
The volume is taken as 1 dm³, so the mass in a whole litre is given rather than in 500 cm³.

mcqs.stem: 4.9 g of sulfuric acid is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 500 cm³. What is the concentration of the solution, in mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of H₂SO₄ = 98)

options.rationale: Amount = 4.9 ÷ 98 = 0.0500 mol, and concentration = 0.0500 ÷ 0.500 dm³ = 0.100 mol/dm³.
The mass is divided by the volume, 4.9 ÷ 0.500, which gives a concentration in g/dm³ labelled as mol/dm³.
The amount is divided by the volume in cm³, 0.0500 ÷ 500, with no conversion to dm³.
The amount is multiplied by 0.500 rather than divided by it, so the rearrangement is inverted.

mcqs.stem: 5.85 g of sodium chloride is dissolved and made up to 250 cm³ of solution. The same mass is dissolved and made up to 1.00 dm³ of solution. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The 1.00 dm³ solution is the more concentrated, because its volume of solution is larger.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read a larger volume of solution as meaning a higher concentration.

options.text: The 250 cm³ solution is the more concentrated, but both hold the same amount of solute.
options.rationale: Both contain 0.100 mol, but that amount is spread through a quarter of the volume, giving 0.400 mol/dm³ against 0.100 mol/dm³.

options.text: The two solutions have the same concentration, because the same mass of solute was used.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think concentration is fixed by the mass weighed out alone.

options.text: The 1.00 dm³ solution must hold four times the amount of solute that the 250 cm³ one holds.
options.rationale: Selected by students who assume a larger volume of solution must contain more dissolved solute.

mcqs.stem: A sodium hydroxide solution has a concentration of 0.250 mol/dm³. What is its concentration in g/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)

options.rationale: The number is carried across unchanged because the two concentration units are treated as equivalent.
The amount is divided by the relative formula mass, 0.250 ÷ 40, instead of multiplied by it.
Each 1 dm³ contains 0.250 mol, and the mass of 0.250 mol is 0.250 × 40 = 10.0 g.
The relative formula mass is quoted as though one mole per dm³ were always dissolved.

mcqs.stem: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution, in mol/dm³?

options.rationale: The known concentration is paired with the wrong volume, giving 0.100 × 0.0250 ÷ 0.0200.
A factor of 2 is applied from the two hydrogen-containing formulae, although the equation is 1:1.
The answer is halved on the assumption that a neutralisation always involves a 2:1 ratio.

mcqs.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 12.5 cm³ of sulfuric acid: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the sulfuric acid, in mol/dm³?

options.rationale: Amount of NaOH = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol; ÷ 2 gives 0.00125 mol of H₂SO₄; 0.00125 ÷ 0.0125 = 0.100 mol/dm³.
The mole ratio is ignored and concentration × volume is simply equated for the two solutions.
The balancing number 2 is used to multiply the amount of acid instead of divide it.
The alkali concentration is halved and quoted directly, with the two volumes never used.

mcqs.stem: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What can be deduced about the two concentrations?

options.text: The acid and the alkali have the same concentration in mol/dm³.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who take equal reacting volumes to mean equal concentrations.

options.text: The concentration of the acid is half the concentration of the alkali.
options.rationale: Equal volumes contain amounts in the ratio of the concentrations, and 1 mol of acid reacts with 2 mol of alkali.

options.text: The concentration of the acid is twice that of the alkali.
options.rationale: The balancing number 2 is applied to the acid rather than to the alkali it belongs to.

options.text: The concentration of the acid is one quarter that of the alkali.
options.rationale: The ratio is squared or the factor 2 applied twice, which is a common response to seeing two 2s in the equation.

mcqs.stem: A student pours 25.0 cm³ from a large bottle of potassium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.200 mol/dm³ into a conical flask. Which statement about the sample in the flask is correct?

options.text: Its concentration is less than 0.200 mol/dm³ because the sample is smaller.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who transfer the reduction in amount across to the concentration.

options.text: Its concentration is 5.00 mol/dm³ because 0.200 × 25.0 cm³ works out at 5.00.
options.rationale: The volume is used in cm³, and the product is then misread as a concentration.

options.text: Its concentration is 0.200 mol/dm³ and it contains 0.00500 mol of solute.
options.rationale: Concentration is a property of the solution, so it is unchanged; the amount is 0.200 × 0.0250 = 0.00500 mol.

options.text: Its concentration is 0.200 g/dm³ and the sample holds 0.00500 g of solute.
options.rationale: Picked by students who use mol/dm³ and g/dm³ as interchangeable units for one value.

mcqs.stem: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 22.5 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution, in g/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)

options.rationale: The mol/dm³ value is given as though it were the g/dm³ value, with no conversion using the relative formula mass.
The concentration is multiplied by 1000, confusing the volume conversion with the change from moles to grams.
The working stops at the amount of solute in moles, which is reported as the concentration.
